1.pericope_label: The finishing of the heavens and the earth, God's rest, and the blessing of the seventh day

schools.summary: Cite the judgment that the chapters are badly divided here and that these verses belong to the first; prefer garniture or ornament to host, on the authority of the Septuagint and Vulgate, and illustrate it by the empty palace and the deserted house; deny that the rest was a cessation, since all things would perish if God withdrew his hand, and confine it to the creation of new kinds; make sanctified exegetical of blessed, sanctifying being separation from the common number; and elsewhere refuse the sixth-day variant, reporting that the change was made for Ptolemy king of Egypt, and read the blessing proleptically with a rabbinic reference forward to the manna.

Read the military sense of host morally — the creatures are numerous but marshalled, disciplined and under command, and every one knows and keeps his place; and hold that God ceased only from creating new species, having in miracles overruled nature without ever changing its settled course, and having rested not as one weary but as one well pleased.

Take host literally as an army under its leaders, applied to the celestial bodies ranged under the sun, and derive the name of the Sabeans from the same word; accept the sixth day of the Septuagint, Syriac and Samaritan as the genuine reading, explaining the corruption by the confusion of the numeral letters vau and zain once written out at length; and expound the blessing lexically as speaking good of and to, so that God has spoken well of the Sabbath and good to those who keep it.

Place these verses with the previous narrative, whose object is to give the Creator's sanction to the Sabbath; deny the military sense of host, referring it to numbers gathered in crowds, whether angels or stars; explain the sixth-day variant as an avoidance of the appearance that Elohim finished creation on the Sabbath; and argue from the blessing being given by Elohim before any covenant that the weekly rest is universal, permanent and independent of the Mosaic law, citing the Accadian sabbath as evidence of its antiquity. Elsewhere take the heading of the following history to begin only at the generations of the heavens and the earth.

debates: Whether the first three verses belong to this chapter or the one before.
Whether the host of them is military, numerical, or ornamental.
Whether the seventh day of verse 2 should be read as the sixth, and how the variant arose.
In what sense God rested, given that he works still.
What blessing and sanctifying a day amount to, and whether the Sabbath precedes the law.
outliers: Clarke alone derives the name of the Sabeans from the word for host.
Calvin alone illustrates the furnished world by an empty palace and a deserted house.
Clarke alone treats the sixth-day reading as genuine and explains it from confusion of numeral letters.
Gill alone passes on the account that the text was altered for Ptolemy king of Egypt.
Ellicott alone appeals to the Accadian sabbath, and alone rests the permanence of the rest on its being given by Elohim rather than Jehovah.
Wesley's note here is an abridgement of Henry's at the same verse, following it phrase for phrase.

4.pericope_label: The generations of the heavens and the earth, the name Jehovah Elohim, and the earth watered by a mist

schools.summary: Read the generations as looking back on the preceding history, creation being a kind of generation and its day a birthday; report the inference drawn from the distribution of the divine names, that Moses compiled older annals, and set against it the argument that each passage requires the very name it uses; explain why the herbs of the third day are named again, namely that they were then produced without seed or root or graft, springing at God's command with a vigour needing neither rain nor culture; and note that the plants were made before any were sown, and that the mist rose once the waters were drained and the earth warmed.

Mark the new name — Elohim a God of power, Jehovah Elohim a God of power and perfection, a finishing God, given when the work is finished as it was given when he performed his promise; and draw the practical inferences that the earth brings forth nothing by its own innate virtue, that rain is a gift withheld or sent or distinguishingly bestowed by God, and that since God is not tied to the means he ordinarily uses we must neither tempt him by neglecting means nor distrust him in the want of them.

Gloss the new name as denoting him that was, and is, and is to come; derive the English word Lord from the Anglo-Saxon for loaf and for supplying, making a lord the dispenser of bread as the old nobility were who kept open house, and apply it to the bread of God which cometh down from heaven; hold that everything was created in a state of maturity and full growth so that man found all ready for his use; and explain the mist meteorologically, as vapours ascending and condensing in colder air and falling back as dew, which is Moses teaching how rain is produced.

Take the generations forward, insisting that what follows is not a second or independent creation account nor a set of appendices but the commencement of the history of the human race and of the place prepared for man's abode; explain the day as the six days viewed as divisions of one continuous act; correct the rendering of verse 5 to say that no wild shrub was yet on the earth and no herb had sprung up, the writer preparing for the planting of paradise, and add that while the earth was hot enough for water to exist only as vapour there could be no vegetation; and identify the mist, from the same word rendered vapour elsewhere, as the measure and material of rain.

debates: Whether the generations of the heavens and the earth look backward or forward.
Why the divine name changes here, and what follows from the change.
Why the plants and herbs are mentioned again after the third day.
How the earth was watered before there was rain.
outliers: Calvin alone reports and weighs the argument that Moses compiled older written annals.
Clarke alone leaves the Hebrew to derive the English word Lord from the giving out of bread.
Ellicott alone appeals to geology, and alone corrects the translation of verse 5 outright.
Clarke alone reads the mist as an account of the physical mechanism of rainfall.
Keil alone states negatively what the following section is not.

7.pericope_label: Man formed of dust and made a living soul, the garden planted in Eden, and the two trees

schools.summary: Identify the verb as the potter's and the matter as red earth mixed with water, and take it as a humbling of pride; hold, against most of the ancients, that living soul denotes the animal life that imparts breath and motion, while the human soul keeps its proper rank; find the mark of man's dignity rather in his being gradually formed where the beasts sprang up in a moment; place Eden in Mesopotamia and allow that eastward may mean before, the planting having been on the third day; reject the rendering in the beginning and refuse to extend the garden over the whole world; and deny that the tree of life could confer life, making it a symbol and memorial of life already received, since God attests his grace by external symbols, and decline to settle whether two trees or two kinds are meant. Note also that the trees gratified sight as well as taste and may emblem the saints.

Leave the geography aside and describe the residence: a garden and not an ivory house, since as clothes came in with sin so did houses, with heaven for its roof, earth for its floor and the shadow of the trees for its rooms, finer than Solomon in all his glory; and explain that the inspired penman, writing for the infant church, describes things by their outward sensible appearances, the Mosaic history holding the patterns of heavenly things rather than the heavenly things themselves.

Build on the plural breath of lives, animal and intellectual, so that the inspiration gave both spirit and understanding and body and soul are shown to be distinct; grant that Eden means pleasure but is a place, and derive the heathen gardens of the Hesperides and of Adonis from the name while leaving the etymology of paradise uncertain; and read the tree of life first as the medicinal plants that keep death at a distance and then as the actual means of preserving the body in continual vital energy, an antidote against death. Join in describing the garden as a palace roofed by heaven and floored by earth.

Observe that the prominent idea here is not creation out of nothing but shaping and moulding, so that Elohim is almighty power and Jehovah wisdom and skill, and that the whole narrative is anthropomorphic; note that the material marks man's feebleness, being not rock or metal but the shifting particles of the surface; deny that living soul carries any idea of spiritual existence, since the animals bear the same phrase, while insisting the life came as a direct gift and not by evolution; take Eden as the proper name of a district meaning delight, distinct from the Edens of Assyria and Coelesyria, and trace Paradise through the Septuagint to a Persian word for a hedged enclosure; dispute whether eastward means the eastern part of Eden or that Eden lay east of Israel; and hold that the tree of life would physically have sustained a naturally mortal body, and that the tree of knowledge can only have been so named after the fall.

debates: What the forming of man out of dust is meant to teach.
Whether living soul denotes anything more than the animal life shared with the beasts.
Where Eden was, and whether eastward describes a part of Eden or its position relative to Israel.
Where the word paradise comes from.
Whether the tree of life sustained life physically or signified it sacramentally.
outliers: Ellicott alone notes that the material is chosen from the surface rather than from rock or ore to mark feebleness.
Clarke alone builds a doctrine of the soul on the plural in the breath of lives.
Keil and Ellicott, of the same school, read eastward in Eden in flatly incompatible ways.
Calvin alone denies the tree of life any physical operation and makes it purely a memorial sign.
Ellicott alone reports that the Chaldean legends identify the tree of life with the plant from which the soma juice is prepared.

10.pericope_label: The river of Eden parted into four heads, and the land of Havilah where there is gold

schools.summary: Catalogue the wild variety of opinions on the site of paradise, from the third heaven and the moon to China, Ceylon and the poles, and refuse the allegorical option because the description is too particular and circumstantial — one might as well allegorise Adam and Eve as their address; then adopt the Armenian reconstruction that places it near the sources of the Euphrates, Tigris, Phasis and Araxes, identifying Pison with the Phasis of Colchis from the city answering to Havilah and Gihon with the Araxes because both names denote rapid motion; and on the two hard words report the guesses that bdellium is the pearl-oyster and shoham the onyx, named from the Greek for a fingernail, while declining to decide at such a distance of time and place.

Refuse the solution that the deluge shifted the springs and courses, since the earth, though cursed and in places laid waste, is the same earth created in the beginning; grant instead that Moses accommodated his topography to the capacity of his age and speaks popularly rather than philosophically, as when he called the moon one of two great luminaries; conclude that the four heads are not four springs, no fountain being mentioned, but the streams above and the mouths below a confluence of the Euphrates with the Tigris, supported from Pliny on the Orcheni, from Pomponius Mela, and from Nearchus reckoning the distance to Babylon, with a map supplied. Elsewhere keep the identifications open — the one river perhaps lost, perhaps the Jordan — deny that Pison is either the Nile or the Ganges since the country suits neither Egypt nor India, prefer the river called Phasis or Pasitigris, and gather the classical reports of Arabian gold that comes from the ground already pure and of the gold-bearing rivers of Colchis that gave rise to the fable of the golden fleece.

Read the tenses as present, as though the features of the country were unchanged, so that one river goes forth from Eden and is parted outside the garden into four main streams; report that this has led many to place the site in a submerged part of the Persian Gulf, where the Babylonian legends locate it at Eridu with the Indus and Nile for the other rivers, and that another suggestion is a Babylonian province where four rivers may be found; object to both on the ground that from there the ark could not have floated against the current up to the highlands of Armenia; and record without endorsing that many authors of note have taken the whole passage symbolically, one Syriac writer reading it as a description of the human body.

debates: Where the garden stood, and whether the question can be answered at all.
Whether the deluge altered the courses of the rivers, or whether the text must be squared with the present geography.
Whether the four heads are four sources or the branches of a confluence.
Which rivers Pison and Gihon are.
Whether the topography is literal or symbolic.
outliers: Clarke alone assembles the whole catalogue of proposed sites in order to discredit the allegorical reading.
Calvin alone refuses the appeal to the deluge and answers instead by the principle that Moses writes popularly.
Calvin alone supplies his readers with a map.
Ellicott alone rules out two proposed sites by asking how the ark could have reached Armenia against the current.
Gill and Clarke arrive at the fable of the golden fleece by different routes, Gill from the gold-bearing rivers of Colchis and Clarke from the identification of Havilah.

13.pericope_label: Gihon, Hiddekel and Euphrates, and the man placed in the garden to dress it and to keep it

schools.summary: Leave the identification of Gihon open among a river near Jerusalem, the Nile, a branch of the Euphrates or Tigris, and the Araxes, deriving the name from coming forth with force; collect the etymology of Hiddekel from the Targum, from Pliny, and from the Persian word for a dart, and then let modern travellers contradict it by reporting the river slow, crooked and choked with islands; insist that the taking of the man was not a corporeal assumption but a leading by the hand, and pass on the traditions that he was made near Damascus or on the temple mount; hold that men were created for work and not for idleness, the labour being pleasant and free from weariness yet condemning all indolent repose; and turn the charge to keep the garden into a doctrine of stewardship, by which a man holds what he has on condition of frugal use, handing his field to posterity as he received it or better cultivated.

Dispose of the identification of Gihon with the Nile on historical grounds, since Cush at this period meant southern Arabia and the name reached Abyssinia only later with colonists, and offer the Oxus or the Araxes instead, noting that the name is a common Arabic word for a river; attack the form of Hiddekel as a startling quadriliteral, preferring the Samaritan reading with the article; argue from the absence of any description of the Euphrates, as the largest and best known river, that Pison and Gihon must have been small streams; observe that the word here rendered put means he made him rest, giving the garden as a permanent dwelling; and hear a warning in the charge to keep it, since though no blight spoiled the crop the garden had to be guarded against wild animals and birds and against wind and burning heat.

Note that gardening is the first employment on record and was undertaken in a state of innocence, that dressing and tilling were needed to maintain the plants and repress luxuriance, and that man could not have been happy inactive, since the structure of his body as well as his mind proves he was never intended for a merely contemplative life.

Observe that the placing of the man in a garden he did not make shuts out all boasting, since only he that made us can make us happy; that none of us were sent into the world to be idle, work being required even in paradise; that those who do their earthly business with an eye to God serve him as truly as when they are on their knees; and that the husbandman's calling is ancient and honourable, there being true pleasure in the business God calls us to.

debates: Which river Gihon is, and whether Cush means Ethiopia or Arabia.
Whether the name Hiddekel really means swift, and whether the word is even correctly transmitted.
What it means that God took the man and put him in the garden.
What the charge to dress and to keep the garden implies about work.
outliers: Gill assembles the traditional etymology of the Tigris and then lets travellers' reports overturn it.
Ellicott alone argues from the silence about the Euphrates that the other two rivers were small.
Calvin alone reads the charge to keep the garden as a doctrine of stewardship owed to posterity.
Ellicott alone finds danger implied in paradise, the garden needing to be guarded against beasts and weather.
Three schools reach the same verdict on idleness by three different routes.

16.pericope_label: The command not to eat of the tree of knowledge, and the declaration that it is not good for man to be alone

schools.summary: Insist that it would have made no difference to God what fruit was eaten, so that the prohibition of one tree was purely a test of obedience and a first lesson in dependence; meet the objection that the law is not made for the righteous by answering that the apostle argues from the common practice of life and does not deny that God imposed a law from the beginning, and that the law is a minister of death only accidentally, through our corruption; generalise the declaration about solitude beyond Adam into the principle that man was formed a social animal, and turn it against those who think celibacy advantageous, whether heathen writers or the fathers who wrote against marriage; and observe that God had the right to command as Creator, benefactor and preserver, that the prohibition bound the woman also, and that the saying about solitude was a purpose formed in God's mind on the sixth day.

Call this the first positive precept, given as proof of a dependent and probationary state, since man was lord of the lower world but only God's vicegerent, and warn that the man in whom that sense of dependence is erased loses sight of his origin and end and is capable of any wickedness, an intelligent creature without a law being an absurdity; render the sentence literally as dying thou shalt die, taking it of spiritual death by the loss of the life of God and of a mortality beginning at once, so that every moment of life is an act of dying; and construe the helper as one like himself standing opposite to him, a perfect resemblance with neither inferiority nor superiority, holding that celibacy is not good on either side whatever men call it. Add that the threatened death means the loss of all happiness in possession and in prospect.

Stress that the man commanded stood as a public person, the father and representative of all mankind, receiving law as he had lately received a nature, for himself and all his, and that the command was no disparagement to his greatness or happiness; read the grant of every other tree as an assurance of immortal life, the tree of life standing in the midst of the garden and being the one thing withdrawn at the revolt; and pity the solitude of a creature set between an upper world of angels and a lower world of brutes with none of his own rank between, since perfect solitude would turn a paradise into a desert and a palace into a dungeon, adding that God could have made a world of men at once but chose a succession of generations beginning from two.

Draw from the words the divine appointment of marriage and the declaration that the female is subsequent in order of production to the male and formed from him, though the first chapter represents the making of male and female as simultaneous, and ground the happiness of marriage not on the woman being the same thing as the man but on his seeing in her his image and counterpart; and take the general word for help to mean a helping being in which the man may recognise himself as soon as he sees it, such help being needed for his whole calling to cultivate and govern the earth and not merely to multiply his race.

debates: Why a prohibition was necessary at all, and what it was a test of.
Whether an innocent man needed a law, given that the law is not made for the righteous.
Whether the threatened death was immediate, spiritual, or gradual.
Whether solitude was bad only for Adam or is bad for men generally.
Whether the helper is the man's equal or his subsequent.
outliers: Calvin alone raises and answers the apostolic objection that the righteous need no law.
Clarke alone argues that a creature capable of reason without a rule of conduct is an absurdity.
Clarke and Ellicott read the same two words to opposite effect on the standing of the woman.
Calvin and Clarke arrive at the same verdict against celibacy from a general principle and from the vocabulary respectively.
Wesley reproduces Henry's observation on the upper and lower worlds almost word for word.

19.pericope_label: The animals brought to the man to be named, and the deep sleep in which the woman was made

schools.summary: Warn that much curious speculation has arisen from mistaking the order of the verses for chronology, as though the animals were made after man and woman called into being only when they failed him, and insist that the real point is the insight given into the man's intellectual condition and daily employment, the assertion that woman alone is meet for him coming last and with cumulative force; deny that a long procession of beasts and birds passed before him to be named, and put in its place a keen observer meeting new creatures as he works, studying their habits, and naming them from their cries or from some marked feature of form, plumage or motion, with the practical end of taming what might be useful, whence reptiles and fish go unmentioned; and observe that the word rendered rib is everywhere else side or flank, as the ancient versions have it, so that woman is one side of the man and the closing of the flesh means only that a cavity was prevented.

Observe that the verb refers to what had already taken place, and that of all the animals set in order none was found adapted to the man, not through ignorance since he named them from certain knowledge; take the bringing to mean that God endued the creatures with a disposition to obedience so that they offered themselves voluntarily, and infer that their gentleness would have continued had man not forfeited his authority, some now being tamed with difficulty and some inspiring terror, though remains of the old subjection persist; note that only the animals nearest man are spoken of, the fishes living as in another world, and that the names given were each well founded though their use is now obsolete; insist that the sleep was supernatural rather than natural weariness, the senses locked so that the operation was painless and the man had no hand in the woman's formation; and answer the scoffers who think the account fabulous or the rib either superfluous or its loss a mutilation, preferring the conjecture that something was taken so that he might embrace a part of himself, losing a rib and gaining a richer reward, both sexes springing from one origin so that he might recognise himself in his wife as in a mirror and she submit willingly as taken out of him. Add that the creatures were formed two and two while man was made single.

Hold that the names in Scripture always express some prominent feature and essential characteristic of the creature, so that without an intuitive knowledge of those properties the man could never have given them — a strong proof of his original perfection, the effect resembling the cause that produced it; and think it immaterial whether rib or side is read, putting the weight instead on this, that God could have formed the woman from the dust as he formed the man, in which case she would have appeared a distinct being to whom he had no natural relation, whereas being of the same identical flesh and blood she has equal powers, faculties and rights.

Give as the reason for the sleep that no room might be left to imagine the man had directed the Spirit of the Lord or been his counsellor, and that while he knows no sin God will take care he shall feel no pain; and reason from the order of events that the man was first formed and then the woman, made of him and for him, which are urged as grounds of submissiveness — while balancing it, since her being made after him and out of him puts an honour on the sex, for if man is the head she is the crown, and the man was dust refined where the woman was dust double-refined, one remove further from the earth.

debates: Whether the order of these verses is chronological, and what the naming of the animals is recorded for.
Whether the creatures were brought in procession or came under the man's notice as he worked.
Whether the names came from intuitive knowledge of the creatures or from their cries and appearance.
Why the man was put to sleep for the making of the woman.
What follows, for the standing of the woman, from her being taken out of the man.
outliers: Calvin has the animals voluntarily offering themselves for inspection; Ellicott denies any such procession took place.
Calvin alone infers from the passage that the ferocity of beasts dates from man's defection.
Ellicott alone doubts the man capable of the discourses a poet gives him.
Clarke alone concludes equal powers, faculties and rights from the woman being taken out of the man.
Ellicott alone insists the word is side and not rib, and that no compensation was given for what was removed.

22.pericope_label: The woman built and brought to the man, the naming of her, the law of marriage, and their nakedness without shame

schools.summary: Note that the verb here is not create or form but build, which suits the woman as the foundation of the house and family, and repeat the observation that she was taken neither from a superior part nor an inferior but from the side, near the heart and under the arm, to be loved and protected; draw from the verse that marriage is divinely instituted, since the man did not take a wife at his own will but received her as offered by God, and name the two contrary artifices by which Satan defames it, the odium that breeds the law of celibacy and the licence claimed within marriage; refuse the explanation that the man guessed the woman's origin by quickness of perception, holding rather that God revealed both the fact and its design, the sleep having been sent to spare him pain and not to hide anything; offer alternatively that he was awake, or had it impressed on his mind, or saw it in a trance; consider whether the marriage law is spoken by God, by the man, or added by Moses as teacher, and most approve the last, while elsewhere judging it God's own on the strength of the Gospel quotation; insist that the husband must prefer his wife even to his father, so that those who allow divorce for slight causes overturn all the laws of nature, and that the singular used throughout confines marriage to two; and ask why the nakedness of a beast disgraces nothing while no one can look on a naked man without shame, answering that in uncorrupted nature there was nothing but what was honourable, so that whatever is opprobrious must be imputed to our own fault. Add that they were no more ashamed than children are.

Press the word built to mean that her formation required time and care, so that woman is no casual or hasty production of nature but the finished result of labour and skill, brought with special honour as the Creator's last and most perfect work, made not from the ground but from the man and bringing back more than he parted with; warn that the anthropomorphic language of these chapters is a condescension to human weakness, and that he who made heaven and earth by the fiat of his will is not to be understood as having moulded the side as a sculptor moulds clay; take the man's exclamation to mean at last, and note that bone stands for self in the Semitic dialects, so that bone of my bones means my very own self while flesh of my flesh adds the gentler qualities; argue that the marriage law is evidently the narrator's words, since the man knew nothing of sons leaving their fathers' houses, and reconcile the Gospel quotation by holding that the narrator was moved by the Spirit to give marriage this solemn sanction; and insist that the closing verse is not the end of the marriage section, where it would be indelicate, but the introduction to the temptation, pointing to the play between the word for naked and the word for crafty.

Render the man's exclamation as this turn, this creature which now passes before me, tying it to the creatures that had passed already and been found unsuitable; give the Latin feminine of man as a parallel to the Hebrew and defend the English word against the folk etymology that makes it man's woe, since the transgression had not yet been committed, and call her a she-man differing from man in sex only and not in nature; hold that the woman's origin was revealed to the man in a vision as he slept; read they two shall be one flesh as the true text, preserved in the versions and lost from the Hebrew by a copyist correcting the wrong verse, and note that the polygamy controversy turns on the numeral; distinguish two senses of one flesh, one body with no separate rights and the production of one flesh in a posterity resembling both; observe that the sabbath and marriage were the two ordinances instituted in innocency, the one for the preservation of the church and the other of mankind; and ground the absence of shame in the absence of sin, since shame can only arise from a consciousness of irregular conduct — blushing being now the colour of virtue though it was not the colour of innocency.

debates: What the change of verb at the building of the woman implies.
How the man knew, having been asleep, that the woman was taken out of him.
What the phrase rendered this now means.
Whether the law of marriage is spoken by God, by the man, or by the narrator.
Whether the words they two belong to the text, and what hangs on it.
Why human nakedness carries shame when that of animals does not.
outliers: Ellicott alone cautions that the language must not be pressed into a picture of God moulding clay like a sculptor.
Calvin alone identifies two opposite satanic attacks on marriage, enforced celibacy and licence.
Clarke ties this now to the procession of animals; Ellicott renders it at last and denies any procession.
Clarke and Calvin defend the same reading against polygamy, one from the versions and one from the singular.
Calvin alone turns the verse about nakedness into a question about the dignity of human nature.
